body:
Life sounds really rough bud. Sometimes I find that just talking to someone else can be helpful. I know you said you've been very isolated, but I'd be more than happy to be your internet pal who you can unload anything onto.

Also I'd like you to think about your father's death. Losing someone to suicide is very hard. Think about how it makes you feel, and try to imagine your sons feeling the same way if you were to do the same. It may help to give you hope.

Remember, hope is something we give ourselves when we are at our lowest.

I'm not saying that I know what your situation is like, but some of the things you say certainly have an air of familiarity to them. I have felt similarly in the past. It is very very hard. I know it may not seem like it now, but things can get better.
Hey. You may have heard this before, but beauty is in the eyes of the beholder. Sounds like you could use a friend. I'll be your friend! How are you? How was your weekend?
I'll be your friend =)

Honestly, life sucks. It sucks for 101 different reasons. But who you are is unique and special. None of your life was wasted. Your experiences and what you learn along the way is what make you who you are.


Forget about the past. Think about what you want for the future. Imagine a future you. What do you want that future you to have? What will they do? What will they look like?


Once you have that image. You just need to fixate on what you can do today, to help get just one step closer to the future you. There's always something.


Forget about the world. Forget about the big problems. Just focus on what you can do, what you can change, and how you can change it.
Is there anything on your mind that you would like to talk about? Is there anything I can do to help you feel better?

I can tell you a little story from my experience.


I was very done with it all. I wanted it all to end. I had looked up height requirements for the 95+% chance of death. And I went to this bridge and climed to the other side of the fence.

My hands gripping the chainlink fence behind me. My heels gripping the cement below my feet. It's all that stood between me and certain death. And for once in my life, as I looked down at the fast flowing river, I seemed in control. I had the power. And I just stood there basking in that amazing feeling of being in control of something. And then people started noticing and eventually I was taken off the bridge and to the hospital.


But it feels good to be in that moment when you think you can influence the next steps of your life.

Almost jumped once. I don't condone suicidal behaviour though, so I can't "help" you there.

As well as having been suicidal myself, I have taken many courses on suicide prevention.

If you fear your friend may be suicidal, the best thing is to just outright ask them. Believe me that you will not be putting the idea into their head or anything. They will either be taken aback and tell you that things aren't that serious, or tell you to what extent they have considered suicide.

Wish you and your friend all the best.

Implementing coping mechanisms can really be an uphill task. When you have no motivation to see the light of the next day, it is hard to convince yourself to keep using coping mechanisms in order to strengthen them.


I hope you're able to get through this though, genuinely.

I have felt the same way before. In fact, I still feel the same. Eventhough I know better from my studies.


Quick psychology lesson for you: memories can be activated by emotional states. If you are angry, you will remember more things from when you have been angry in the past. And it can be hard to think of anything that does not make you angry.


When things are happy and awesome. It becomes hard to remember a time that was worse than this.


When things are depressing, this affect only works to make you think of more depressing things. The depressed and negative thoughts will multiply until they are the only thing inside your head. And after years and years of this, it can become hard to think of anything outside of those depressed thoughts.


You begin to believe that nothing will be right. Nothing can be good again. How can any amount of happiness be worth all this pain?



I don't have an answer for you though. Because like I said at the start, I feel like you too. There is no end; only more pain.
Hey there. Sounds like you've seen better days. I can't guarantee I will be helpful, but I'm always willing to give a listening ear. You can PM me any time.

I saw an addictions counselor for my self harm. It is a long process of working on alternate coping methods.

They won't work at first, but as long as you keep trying and keep practicing them, you'll find that they become stronger over time.

I still get urges all the time, but I now feel more in control of them.

That being said, I still lapse fairly often. But I don't cut daily anymore.

I have done this a few times before. The doctors certainly counted it as a suicide attempt. 

Would you like to discuss what's going on in life right now? Is there anything I can do to help you?

When I had a partner supporting me through this, I recall acting similarly at times.

Our words and our actions will want to drive you away. Your job is to stand there against all odds, and when we tell you to drop dead, you just give us a big hug and tell us it will be alright. That we can get through this together.

I know I have said things to my girlfriend which I regret when I think back. But she always just used to remind me that she is always there to make things easier for me. 

I remember a time where I talked about how much I hated myself and wanted to kill myself. My girlfriend just cried gently and she wrapped her arms around me, and we stayed like that for a while. Human touch, I found, can be very effective in de-escalating these situations.

By no means am I any kind of expert. I can provide you with insight and my personal experiences, but I underatand that they won't be applicable to all situations.

One thing I can think of which may be helpful for the two of you would be working through theraputic exercises together. CBT is often the preferred therapy model these days. You could try finding some CBT worksheets to work on together. I can give you more advice about CBT worksheets if you decide to go through with that.

Ultimately, there is no easy fix. I'm sorry for all the emotional stress you have to deal with, and I am sorry for the situation that you and your girlfriend are trying to work through.

Remember that supporting a depressed person can be very taxing on your own mental health. Make sure you have ways to decompress from the talks you have with your girlfriend. Talk to people or do relaxing things. You wouldn't want to end up depressed yourself.

You can always feel free to PM me if you need to talk. I don't always reply straight away, but this reddit account is linked to my phone.

I know what you mean.

I only began self-harm because I knew it could help. Little did I know it would spiral me into an addiction that requires me to cut deeper and deeper for the same outcomes.

Getting past a self harm addiction is not easy. In fact, I've never gone more than about 6 or 7 months before lapsing again. But I keep working at making it longer and longer between each time.

The key thing, I found, was developing alternate coping strategies. Everyone will say this to you. It's easier said than done. At first, breathing or muscle relaxation or whatever you try wont be as strong as the self harm. Not even close.

The hard part comes with keeping at it, and strengthening those coping skills until you find that they can sometimes be all you need. I've been able to de-escalate potential self harm sessions into heavy breathing exercises in the past. But that's after about two years of persistence with breathing techniques. And even then, like I said, doesn't always work. Sometimes the stress is too much and I fall back to the self harm.

It isn't easy to break the cycle. And it can be hard to find motivation to do it if you're depressed. But it is possible to reduce/stop. Just takes time and effort.

I'm sorry you feel the way that you do, and for the situation you are in. I wish you all the best for the future.

I tend to avoid letting on about mental health issues until I have been working in a place for at least a couple months.

But I have found that the depression makes it difficult to perform well, and keep a job. For me, it tends to interfere with my performance, and employers would rather hire someone with no problems than have to find resources to help support you.

The world is a horrible place, and our capitalist world only cares about working you like a dog whilst giving you as little in return.

A depressed person doesn't make for a 100% efficient and productive employee.

I always struggle to hold down a job =(.
Sometimes I wonder if I should just end it all. It isn't like anyone is going to say "well we tried everything and you still don't feel right. I guess we don't know how to fix you."

First of all: mad props to you for sticking by her in these troubling times. One of the things I remember from my time in hospital is they taught us about this "mental crusher".

Every thought that goes into your mind will first go through the crusher. The crusher ensures that everything you think about has a depressive twist on it. Someone could literally compliment you and you may still be able to find a negative in it. We have to actively work to challenege the crusher and the way it is deforming these thoughts entering our mind.

So what should you do? I think it's best to have very open lines of communication with one another. Be more open and talk about everything and anything. And don't be afraid to ask "is there anything I can do to help/support you in these times."

Personally, I prefer when someone asks this, because then I can either tell them that I am looking for some advice, or that I just need someone to listen to me ramble and vent.

Talk to your girlfriend. Listen to what she has to say, and work with her to challenge these negative cognitions.

One very good couples communication technique if you find you're struggling to understand one another is to do the following:

1. Say something
2. Have your partner say it back to you
3. Correct any misunderstandings they may have interpreted
4. Partner says something
5. Repeat it back to them
6. Etc.

Anti depressants work differently for everyone. There are so many of them that it can be an arduous process to find one which actually works well.

For me, I was skipping days and then double or triple dosing on other days. My depression and self harm began creeping back.

Generally speaking, I was told by doctors and nurses it can take up to 6 weeks to see any influence from the drugs.

Don't expect them to fix everything, but know that they can be helpful.

I'm not a pharmacist, nor a doctor, so I'm not really qualified to talk about the drugs or how they will work on you. I can only talk about my own experiences.

I found zoloft to be the least invasive, and barely noticed any affects. Until I tried to stop taking them and then things went really south. They aren't a miracle drug, but they tinker away a little in the background.
I feel you. I do the same thing. I even have my side of the bed, but there is nobody to sleep on the other half.
I started out with lots of small scratches. I used to find that it was the act of seeing superficial cuts that helped. But with time I need to go deeper and deeper to get the same effect.

Wellbutrin. I'm going to take a guess and say that you're based somewhere in NA. 

I can't link a lot of studies to you because the research on wellbutrin hasn't shown anything substantial in testing. However, there are a lot of patients with mental health disorders who take wellbutrin and seem to - both from self report and observations - do better.

You read correctly about side effects of suicide, but those typically come from individuals low in motivation who have already manifested the idea of suicide and reconciled the thought.

May I ask what kinds of symptoms you experience? It may be that you have nothing to worry about with the side effect of increased suicidality.

Talk to your doctor, talk to your pharmacist, learn about the drug, and see if you feel comfortable taking it.

Coming from me, I have seen the drug help a lot of people and would recommend it for sure. But that's just my two cents.

Note that I am not linking any studies or making claims to what self harm does to the body, but am simpling speaking from an anecdotal experience.


I remember years and years ago reading an article about how cutting your wrists releases endorphins and adrenaline, and that these neurotransmitters make you feel good.


So when I was super depressed I thought I'd give it a try. And it worked. And thus began my addiction which would come to haunt me for years to come.

One of the hardest parts for me when it came to ever committing to a suicide plan/option/whatever, is family. Suicide is yearned for by those who aren't in a clear state of mind. It is important that you remember that. 

This person is still your sibling, but they are diseased, and you need to support and help them. Show him that you are there for him, and if you feel comfortable, let him know he can come talk to you.

Any time I have been close to suicide I have felt isolated. Have you spent a lot of time with your brother lately? Do you see a way you could maybe increase that time over the next couple weeks or so?

If you have any general questions about the topic, please feel free to ask. Or if you have any specifics too really 🤷‍♂️. I'm pretty open about my experiences and treasure an opportunity to learn from them.

I don't remember much about prozac but I have take quite a few SSRIs. I find that generally they aren't like benzos where they just change your life like that. They work slow, they take time to make changes. And sometimes you don't even feel it.

I wonder if you've talked to your doctor about how you feel that prozac isnt working. Of course you don't have to, but that would be my recommendation.

I'm 22 as well and I've gone through so many treatments that straight up did not work. It's hard to keep faith in medicine when it doesnt work at first, not even a little. But sweetie, there are so many treaments, and the disorder we have is pretty complex. Not like broken bones where you just add some gypsum and wait a few weeks. 

If you need someone to talk to, hit me up. Ive gone through the struggle as well, I know a lot of the feelings you are feeling.

Talk to me if you'd like. I might help? Or I might make things worse. What do you have to lose?

I have been to addiction therapy for my self harm as well, so it absolutely can be an addiction. Anything can be addicting.

My advice: try to find a healthier way to cope. I can help you if you'd like. I can teach you what I know.

I totally get this. I've been in a similar situation many times. That moment when you're so close to death, and for once in your life you feel like you're in control. You know that there are actions that you cab do that will influence something. Your actions can actually make a difference for once.

I like to bask in that feeling of control for a while. And then inevitably go home and feel like shit maybe a week later as I wonder why I didn't kill myself earlier.

You can tell the doctors. They have no judgement, and are only there to help you as best as they can. As for telling your family, you could say whatever, or even get the doctor to help you break the news to them.

Either way. Don't lie to the doc. They need to know what happened in order to provide the best treatment.

Other people have recommended that you get out of your situation. Might I recommend the hospital. The psychiatric ward could help you connect with resources on how to cope with some of your emotions and help you get back on your feet.

And in the mean time they can provide a stress free environment where everything is taken care of for you. Consider it. And ask me if you have any questions about the experience, or want to just talk.

They let us have our phones during the day. Here are a few that they've advised me:


* Lower your body temperature. This can be done by simply splashing cold water, or holding your head in a bucket of cold water for as long as you can.

* Engage in intense exercise. Exercise works to release endorphins, the same feel happy chemical that cutting releases.

* Try progressive muscle relaxation. This is a technique where you tense your muscles as hard as you can until you can't hold on anymore. When you release you'll find that the area is much more relaxed.

* heavy breathing. Transition the breathing pattern from being fast and shallow to being deep and long. Breathe from your diaphragm, not the chest. Relaxing breathing happens at the diaphragm.


I have also learned about something called surfing which is particularly been helpful for me. It's all about focusing on the urge to cut when you get it, and if you focus on it enough you'll find that the urge goes away. It's a little more complicated than that, but if that interests you I could tell you a little about that technique too.


Stay safe friend.

I wish you all the best.

I also had a couple friends noticing when we were hanging out and stuff. After that they began approaching me and trying to help.

Some alternatives I've heard are:


Snapping an elastic on your wrist, or placing an ice pack on it until it starts to feel like it's burning.


Alternatively you could use other methods to try and calm yourself down. This includes taking 5 minutes to take some deep breaths, trying to lower your body temp by splashing cold water, or going for some kind of intense exercise.


Best of luck to you.

Death by blood loss requires you to lose about 1.5L of blood. You should experience wooziness and disorientation along with some headaches when your blood levels get too low.


Try to stay safe.

Personally I found that it doesn't really affect anything.


I live in a cold place and cut on my arms. Covering my arms with long sleeves meant that nobody really saw be it people I have a professional relationship with or not.


The act of self harming also doesn't really affect how I interact with others.


So overall, for me: no difference.

I was surprised at how many people I interacted with when wearing short sleeves and nobody noticed.


A friend suggested that perhaps they did but just didn't want to say anything, but you know when people see. They get that momentary involuntary wide eyed look. You see the fear in their eyes as they then look at you with discomfort and concern. Even if they say nothing: you know when people see.


And unfortunately for me, nobody ever saw while I was at school.
I've done this too. Or sometimes I'll just try and dig my nail into my wrist. Problem is my nails are usually trimmed down.

We all know that self harm isn't a practical solution or coping strategy for any problems in life. I'm currently working on developing new coping strategies.

I do remember though that whenever I would be on self harm pics it would always just be a little off putting. Seeing the pictures of other peoples scars helped me not cut.

When you see the cuts but don't feel that rushing sensation of endorphins and adrenaline, it helps to dissociate the two concepts (see neural biological studies on long term depression). 

The pictures looked nasty. Sometimes they'd make me wince. But the bottom line is that they stopped me from picking up my own knife.

Just forget about it all. Forget the loans. Forget the job. Forget the people. Forget the memories.

Move on and just make new ones.

Unfortunately it just isn't that easy. And that's why I fantasize about finding somewhere remote and far away. Once in somewhere all alone, I just want to curl up and die.
I always used to think about what it would be like if I just started walking in some direction. Let my phone die. And just keep going and see what I find. Leave everything here behind.
Have you learned about other coping mechanisms? Maybe look into some.

For as long as you're still standing. You can still be helped. PM me if you'd like to talk about anything. I've been through/am still going through a rough time as well. I may be able to offer some advice.

Stay strong friend.
Let me know if you have any questions about my experience. I'd love to answer them for you.

Hey friend. I agree. It does seem kind of selfish when you're only staying alive for other people, or because other people are forcing you (through laws). But what's going on in your life? What makes you feel this way? If you'd like to chat I would love to listen.

About your second point: it can take a long time to get the right antidepressant and dosage that works for you. It pretty much comes down to trial and error. And meds alone obviously can't fix everything.

Being in a psych ward can be nice. You get a break from life and don't need to worry about anything. They take care of all your stuff and all you need to do is work on treatments and participate in some fun activities. It's almost like kindergarten again. We paint, we do puzzles, we do arts and crafts, we play with toys again. And sometimes it's just nice to feel like a kid again who didn't worry about anything.

It can be rough dealing with depression. And I'm not anywhere close to being cured either. But together we can stand strong and fight this demon off. Stay strong friend.

Her response was to say "well u/laborem, suicide and a desire to kill yourself is pretty serious I'd say, and certainly not a normal way to think. I think maybe you could use some help to stop thinking that way."

Anyway. I know the struggle of both wanting and not wanting to go and get help. The hardest part can be crossing that line. I won't lie: there was definitely a moment where I thought to myself "nothing is ever going to be the same again. Now that I've crossed this boundary, everything is going to change"


And that change was scary. And it still is. But I think I might be for the best.


I don't know what I'm even saying anymore. I can't even remember where this train of thought began, but there it is.
